intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Wolfram syndrome-2 (WFS2) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CISD2 gene (611507) on chromosome 4q24.

checks.claim: Wolfram syndrome-2 (WFS2) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CISD2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous mutation in a novel zinc-finger protein, ERIS, is responsible for Wolfram syndrome 2.
checks.explanation: Title states it; ZCD2 is the alias of CISD2.

checks.claim: The CISD2 gene is located on chromosome 4q24.
checks.evidence_quote: were mapped to the WFS2 locus at 4q22-25
checks.explanation: Abstract places the locus at 4q22-25; 4q24 is the gene's standard location.

paragraphs.text: Wolfram syndrome-2 is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. Its main features are early-onset insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and sensorineural hearing loss. It differs from the classic WFS1-related Wolfram syndrome in two ways. Diabetes insipidus is absent. Patients also have upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding, and defective platelet aggregation.

checks.claim: Wolfram syndrome-2 is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Wolfram syndrome, which is sometimes referred to as "DIDMOAD" (diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and deafness), is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder
checks.explanation: This describes Wolfram syndrome in general, not the 4q-linked form (WFS2) specifically.

checks.claim: A main feature of Wolfram syndrome-2 is early-onset insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.
checks.evidence_quote: only insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy are necessary to make the diagnosis
checks.explanation: Insulin-dependent diabetes is a required diagnostic feature, but the abstract does not say it starts early.

checks.claim: A main feature of Wolfram syndrome-2 is optic atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: only insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy are necessary to make the diagnosis
checks.explanation: Optic atrophy is a required diagnostic feature of Wolfram syndrome in general; the abstract does not describe it for the 4q-linked families specifically.

checks.claim: A main feature of Wolfram syndrome-2 is sensorineural hearing loss.
checks.evidence_quote: Sensorineuronal Deafness | X | X | X
checks.explanation: Table 3 lists sensorineural deafness in WFS2, and this patient had sensorineural hearing loss.

checks.claim: Unlike classic WFS1-related Wolfram syndrome, Wolfram syndrome-2 lacks diabetes insipidus.
checks.evidence_quote: There is an absence of diabetes insipidus in all affected family members.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

checks.claim: Unlike classic WFS1-related Wolfram syndrome, patients with Wolfram syndrome-2 have upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition, several patients have profound upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

checks.claim: Unlike classic WFS1-related Wolfram syndrome, patients with Wolfram syndrome-2 have defective platelet aggregation.
checks.evidence_quote: The clinical phenotype of WFS2 differs from WFS1 for the absence of diabetes insipidus and psychiatric disorders, and for the presence of bleeding upper intestinal ulcers and defective platelet aggregation.
checks.explanation: The paper lists defective platelet aggregation as a feature that distinguishes WFS2 from WFS1.

paragraphs.text: El-Shanti et al. (2000) studied consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome. Affected individuals had juvenile-onset diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and hearing loss, but no diabetes insipidus. Several also had upper gastrointestinal ulcers with bleeding.

checks.claim: El-Shanti et al. (2000) studied consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: To pursue the possibility of locus heterogeneity, 16 patients from four different families were recruited.
checks.explanation: The abstract says the patients came from four families but does not say they were Jordanian or consanguineous.

checks.claim: Affected individuals in the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) had juvenile-onset diabetes mellitus.
checks.evidence_quote: These patients, who have the Wolfram syndrome phenotype, also have additional features that have not previously been reported.
checks.explanation: Diabetes is implied by the Wolfram diagnosis, but the abstract does not say it was juvenile-onset or give an age of onset.

checks.claim: Affected individuals in the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) had optic atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: These patients, who have the Wolfram syndrome phenotype, also have additional features that have not previously been reported.
checks.explanation: Optic atrophy is implied by the Wolfram diagnosis but is not stated explicitly for these patients.

checks.claim: Affected individuals in the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) had hearing loss.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not report hearing loss in these patients.

checks.claim: Affected individuals in the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) did not have diabetes insipidus.
checks.evidence_quote: There is an absence of diabetes insipidus in all affected family members.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly; only the 'Jordanian' description is not in the abstract.

checks.claim: Several affected individuals in the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) had upper gastrointestinal ulcers with bleeding.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition, several patients have profound upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) studied the same Jordanian families further. They described a bleeding tendency and defective platelet aggregation, as well as peptic ulcer disease, in affected members.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) further studied the same Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families previously studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000).
checks.evidence_quote: It had been shown that these families did not have mutations in the WFS1 gene (WFS1) but were mapped to the WFS2 locus at 4q22-25.
checks.explanation: The abstract implies the families were studied before but does not name El-Shanti et al. (2000).

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) described a bleeding tendency in affected members of the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome-2 families.
checks.explanation: Only the abstract was supplied. It does not mention a bleeding tendency.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) described defective platelet aggregation in affected members of the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome-2 families.
checks.explanation: Only the abstract was supplied. It does not mention platelet aggregation.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) described peptic ulcer disease in affected members of the Jordanian Wolfram syndrome-2 families.
checks.explanation: Only the abstract was supplied. It does not mention peptic ulcer disease.

paragraphs.text: WFS2 is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. This was shown by its occurrence in consanguineous families (El-Shanti et al., 2000) and by the homozygous mutation found by Amr et al. (2007).

checks.claim: WFS2 is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
checks.evidence_quote: is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder
checks.explanation: The abstract calls Wolfram syndrome in general autosomal recessive, not WFS2 specifically.

checks.claim: WFS2 occurs in consanguineous families, supporting autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not mention consanguinity. Homozygosity mapping implies it, but the abstract does not say so.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) found a homozygous mutation in WFS2 patients, supporting autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous mutation in a novel zinc-finger protein, ERIS, is responsible for Wolfram syndrome 2.
checks.explanation: The homozygous mutation is stated, and it is consistent with recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: El-Shanti et al. (2000) ran a genomewide linkage analysis in consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome. They mapped a second Wolfram syndrome locus to chromosome 4q22-q24. Linkage to the WFS1 region on 4p16 was excluded in these families.

checks.claim: El-Shanti et al. (2000) performed a genomewide linkage analysis in consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: For the other three families, genetic heterogeneity for Wolfram syndrome was verified by demonstration of linkage to chromosome 4q22-24.
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms a linkage analysis, but it does not call it genomewide or describe the families as Jordanian or consanguineous.

checks.claim: El-Shanti et al. (2000) mapped a second Wolfram syndrome locus to chromosome 4q22-q24.
checks.evidence_quote: genetic heterogeneity for Wolfram syndrome was verified by demonstration of linkage to chromosome 4q22-24
checks.explanation: The abstract states the 4q22-24 locus directly.

checks.claim: El-Shanti et al. (2000) excluded linkage to the WFS1 region on chromosome 4p16 in the consanguineous Jordanian Wolfram syndrome families.
checks.evidence_quote: we significantly excluded linkage in three of the four families. The two affected individuals in one family showed homozygosity for all three markers from the region of linkage on chromosome 4p16.1.
checks.explanation: Linkage to 4p16 was excluded in only three of the four families. One family was homozygous for all three markers in that region.

paragraphs.text: The families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) did not show linkage to the WFS1 locus on 4p16. This showed that Wolfram syndrome is genetically heterogeneous.

checks.claim: The Wolfram syndrome families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) did not show linkage to the WFS1 locus on 4p16.
checks.evidence_quote: we significantly excluded linkage in three of the four families. The two affected individuals in one family showed homozygosity for all three markers from the region of linkage on chromosome 4p16.1.
checks.explanation: This holds for three of the four families only; one family was homozygous for all three markers in the 4p16.1 region.

checks.claim: The lack of linkage to WFS1 in the families studied by El-Shanti et al. (2000) showed that Wolfram syndrome is genetically heterogeneous.
checks.evidence_quote: For the other three families, genetic heterogeneity for Wolfram syndrome was verified by demonstration of linkage to chromosome 4q22-24.
checks.explanation: The paper establishes heterogeneity by showing positive linkage to 4q22-24, not only by the absence of linkage to WFS1.

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) studied the Jordanian families with WFS2 linked to 4q22-q24. They found a homozygous mutation in the CISD2 gene (also called ZCD2), which encodes the protein ERIS. The mutation was predicted to change a single amino acid. However, it also disrupted splicing, so that exon 2 was skipped and the protein lost its function. The mutation segregated with the disease in these families.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) studied Jordanian families with WFS2 linked to chromosome 4q22-q24.
checks.evidence_quote: were mapped to the WFS2 locus at 4q22-25
checks.explanation: The abstract gives 4q22-25, not 4q22-q24.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) found a homozygous mutation in the CISD2 gene (also called ZCD2) in the Jordanian WFS2 families.
checks.evidence_quote: A single missense mutation was identified in a novel, highly conserved zinc-finger gene, ZCD2, in three consanguineous families of Jordanian descent
checks.explanation: The title confirms the mutation is homozygous.

checks.claim: The CISD2 gene encodes the protein ERIS.
checks.evidence_quote: The ZCD2-encoded protein, ERIS (endoplasmic reticulum intermembrane small protein)
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: The CISD2 mutation found by Amr et al. (2007) was predicted to cause a single amino acid substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: A G-->C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicts an amino acid change from glutamic acid to glutamine (E37Q).
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: The CISD2 mutation found by Amr et al. (2007) disrupted splicing, causing skipping of exon 2.
checks.evidence_quote: The mutation was found to disrupt messenger RNA splicing by eliminating exon 2
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: The CISD2 mutation found by Amr et al. (2007) resulted in loss of protein function.
checks.evidence_quote: The mutation was found to disrupt messenger RNA splicing by eliminating exon 2, and it results in the introduction of a premature stop codon.
checks.explanation: A premature stop codon implies loss of function, but the abstract does not say so explicitly.

checks.claim: The CISD2 mutation found by Amr et al. (2007) segregated with WFS2 in the Jordanian families.
checks.explanation: Segregation is not mentioned in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2009) found that mice lacking Cisd2 showed signs of premature aging. These included mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction, loss of nerve and muscle tissue, and a shortened lifespan. This suggested that CISD2 is needed to keep mitochondria intact.

checks.claim: Chen et al. (2009) found that Cisd2-deficient mice showed signs of premature aging.
checks.evidence_quote: Cisd2 deficiency drives premature aging and causes mitochondria-mediated defects in mice.
checks.explanation: The title and abstract state that Cisd2 deficiency produces phenotypes suggestive of premature aging.

checks.claim: Cisd2-deficient mice showed mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: Cisd2 deficiency in mice causes mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction accompanied by autophagic cell death
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Cisd2-deficient mice showed loss of nerve and muscle tissue.
checks.evidence_quote: these events precede the two earliest manifestations of nerve and muscle degeneration
checks.explanation: The abstract reports nerve and muscle degeneration in the knockout mice.

checks.claim: Cisd2-deficient mice had a shortened lifespan.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we show for the first time that CISD2 is involved in mammalian life-span control.
checks.explanation: The abstract says CISD2 is involved in life-span control and that the mice age prematurely, but it never explicitly reports a shortened lifespan or survival data. Those may be in the full text, which was not supplied.

checks.claim: Chen et al. (2009) concluded that CISD2 is required to maintain mitochondrial integrity.
checks.evidence_quote: Our study also reveals that Cisd2 is primarily localized in the mitochondria and that mitochondrial degeneration appears to have a direct phenotypic consequence that triggers the accelerated aging process in Cisd2 knockout mice
checks.explanation: The abstract implies this, since Cisd2 sits in mitochondria and its loss causes mitochondrial breakdown. It never actually states the conclusion that CISD2 is required to maintain mitochondrial integrity.

clinical_synopsis.hpo_label: Bleeding with minor or no trauma

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) studied affected members of consanguineous Jordanian families with WFS2. They found a homozygous c.109G-C transversion in the CISD2 gene, predicting a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution. The change caused aberrant splicing with loss of exon 2, and the transcript lost its function.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) studied affected members of consanguineous Jordanian families with WFS2.
checks.evidence_quote: in three consanguineous families of Jordanian descent with Wolfram syndrome (WFS)
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: Affected members of the Jordanian WFS2 families carried a homozygous c.109G-C transversion in the CISD2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A G-->C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicts an amino acid change from glutamic acid to glutamine (E37Q).
checks.explanation: The title confirms the mutation is homozygous.

checks.claim: The CISD2 c.109G-C transversion is predicted to cause a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: A G-->C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicts an amino acid change from glutamic acid to glutamine (E37Q).
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: The CISD2 c.109G-C change caused aberrant splicing with loss of exon 2.
checks.evidence_quote: the pathogenesis for the disorder is because the mutation also causes aberrant splicing. The mutation was found to disrupt messenger RNA splicing by eliminating exon 2
checks.explanation: Stated.

checks.claim: The CISD2 c.109G-C change resulted in a transcript that lost its function.
checks.evidence_quote: it results in the introduction of a premature stop codon
checks.explanation: Loss of function is implied by the premature stop codon but not stated explicitly.
